title: Rend Your Hearts: The Day, the Return, and the Spirit
summary: The alarm sounds in Zion as an unstoppable army, led by the LORD himself, darkens the land. Yet God calls his people to return to him with all their heart, because he is gracious and compassionate, and Joel summons everyone to a sacred assembly. The LORD answers with pity: he will drive away the northern army, restore the harvests, repay the years the locusts ate, and afterward pour out his Spirit on all people, so that everyone who calls on his name will be saved.
story: Chapter 1 described a locust plague and named it a sign of the Day of the LORD. Chapter 2 brings that Day into full view and then reaches the turning point of the whole book. The same prophet who sounded the alarm also announces that it is not too late: "Yet even now" God invites his people back. Their return opens the way for God's answer, which moves outward in widening circles, from rain and grain to the gift of his Spirit on every kind of person. The chapter carries the story forward from a single disaster in Judah to a promise the New Testament says began to be fulfilled at Pentecost.
historical:
As with the rest of Joel, the historical setting cannot be pinned down with certainty, and the book's date is debated (see the introduction). The chapter assumes a functioning temple in Jerusalem with its altar and its portico, the porch at the front of the sanctuary, and priests who could lead a public fast. The call to gather even nursing infants and newly married couples (verse 16) shows a crisis grave enough to override every other obligation; the law normally excused a new husband from military service for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5).

Interpreters differ over the army of verses 1 to 11. Many read it as the locusts of chapter 1 described as a military force, since the details (appearance like horses, climbing walls, entering windows) fit locust swarms closely. Others see a human invader, perhaps Assyrian or Babylonian, described in locust imagery, pointing to the "northern army" of verse 20, since Israel's great invaders came from the north. Still others read the army as an end-time force, the ultimate expression of the Day of the LORD. The imagery deliberately blurs these categories, and each reading has able defenders.
cultural:
The ram's horn (shofar) was blown to sound alarms in war and to summon the people to sacred gatherings; in verse 1 it does the first, in verse 15 the second. Tearing one's garments was a traditional sign of grief or shock (Genesis 37:34; 2 Samuel 1:11). Joel's call to "rend your hearts and not your garments" does not abolish the outward sign but demands that it express a real inward change. The priests were to weep "between the portico and the altar", the space in the temple courtyard where they ordinarily ministered.

The rains of verse 23 were the lifeblood of Judah's farming year. The early or autumn rains (roughly October and November) softened the ground for plowing and sowing, and the late or spring rains (roughly March and April) filled out the grain before harvest. The word translated "autumn rains" in verse 23 can also mean teacher, and some interpreters read the phrase as the teacher for righteousness; most translations prefer rain in context. The Eastern Sea and Western Sea (verse 20) are the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean. Locust swarms that died in the sea could wash ashore and rot, which may explain the stench of verse 20.
literary: The chapter has two halves. Verses 1 to 17 continue the call to alarm and repentance: a vivid description of the invading army (verses 1 to 11) is followed by the call to return (verses 12 to 14) and to assemble (verses 15 to 17). Verse 18 is the hinge: "Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people." Verses 19 to 32 are God's answer, reversing chapter 1 point by point: grain, new wine, and oil return, the fig and vine bear fruit, the beasts that panted for water find green pasture, and the four locust names are listed again (verse 25) as God promises to repay what they destroyed. Verse 13 quotes the ancient confession of God's character from Exodus 34:6, which also appears in Jonah 4:2 and Psalm 103:8. In the Hebrew Bible, verses 28 to 32 form a separate chapter (chapter 3).

outline.t: The alarm: the Day of the LORD and its army
Yet even now: return with all your heart
A sacred assembly and the priests' prayer
The LORD takes pity and drives the northern army away
Rejoice: rain, harvest, and the years restored
The Spirit poured out and salvation for all who call

doctrines.note: Verses 12 and 13 are one of Scripture's clearest calls to repent: return to God with all your heart, with outward signs that express an inner change. Joel roots the call in God's character rather than in the people's ability to earn forgiveness.

Joel repeats the confession that God is "gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" and adds that he "relents from sending disaster". Yet the prophet does not presume: "Who knows? He may turn and relent." God's mercy is certain, but it is never owed.

Verses 28 and 29 promise that the Spirit, once given to particular leaders and prophets, will be poured out on all people without regard to age, sex, or social standing. Peter announced at Pentecost that this promise had begun to be fulfilled (Acts 2:16-18).

Verse 32 opens salvation to "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD". Paul quotes it in Romans 10:13 to show that there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile: the same Lord is Lord of all and generous to all who call on him.

words.note: Qara, to tear or rend. It is the verb for tearing clothes in mourning. Joel keeps the gesture but moves it inward: "rend your hearts and not your garments". The heart in Hebrew thought is the center of will and thought, not only of feeling, so this is a call to change one's whole direction.

Nacham, in this context to relent or change course, often translated repent when used of God. Scripture teaches that God does not change his character or purposes, yet it also describes him as relenting from announced judgment when people turn (Jeremiah 18:7-8). Joel appeals to this responsive mercy.

Ruach, spirit, also meaning breath or wind. In the Old Testament the Spirit of the LORD comes on judges, kings, and prophets to empower them. Joel's promise that God will pour it out "on all people" (literally, all flesh) widens that gift beyond anything Israel had known.

Moreh, which can mean the early (autumn) rain or a teacher, from a root meaning to throw, shoot, or direct. In verse 23 the context of rain and harvest favors "autumn rains", but the double meaning has long interested interpreters, and some read a promise of a teacher of righteousness.

christ: On the day of Pentecost, fifty days after Jesus's resurrection, the Holy Spirit came on the disciples in Jerusalem, and they spoke in other languages. Peter explained, "this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16), and quoted verses 28 to 32. He then preached Jesus as the crucified and risen one who, exalted to God's right hand, had received the promised Spirit and poured it out (Acts 2:33). Peter ended his quotation with Joel's promise of salvation for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord, and he identified that Lord as Jesus (Acts 2:21, 36). Paul does the same in Romans 10:9-13. The chapter's call to return with the whole heart also anticipates the preaching of repentance by John the Baptist and Jesus, and its picture of a God who relents and restores prepares for the gospel's announcement of grace.

hard.q: Peter said Joel's prophecy was fulfilled at Pentecost, but the sun did not turn dark or the moon to blood that day. How does that work?
hard.a: Interpreters answer in several ways. Some note that the sun was darkened at Jesus's crucifixion only weeks earlier (Luke 23:44-45) and suggest Peter saw the cosmic signs as already under way. Others read the signs as traditional prophetic imagery for God's decisive intervention in history, language of upheaval rather than astronomical prediction, as when Isaiah uses similar images for the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10). Many see the fulfillment as beginning at Pentecost and completed at Christ's return: the Spirit's outpouring marks the start of the last days, and the cosmic signs belong to the great Day that is still to come. These views can overlap, and they share the conviction that Peter was right to see Joel's promised age of the Spirit arriving in the church. What Peter clearly stressed was the Spirit's arrival and the offer of salvation, not a timetable of heavenly signs.

questions: Joel says, "rend your hearts and not your garments". What outward religious habits can become a substitute for inward change, and how can they instead express it?
The call to return rests on God's character: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger. How does knowing what God is like make it easier, or harder, to come back to him?
God promises to pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, old and young, servants and free. What does that suggest about who God uses and how the church should see one another?
